acv.quote: The account was worth about three hundred and twenty K a year.

header.scope: Lost: the international business split off to local acquiring; the US stayed with us.
header.tag_why: The new head of payments compared country-by-country approval results, Adyen's test on his international traffic against our average-uplift deck, and our own per-market analysis arrived after the test was finished.

evidence.excerpt: A new head of payments. Stefan. They'd never had one.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: Payments sat under an engineering manager, the guy who originally bought us, and he left last year.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: the first thing he did was pull declines by country. A few of their international markets looked bad to him.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: No. I knew the engineering manager had left. I didn't know they'd hired a head of payments.
evidence.label: fact

trigger.insight: The trigger was a change of buyer, not a product failure. The engineer who bought us for developer reasons was replaced by a payments specialist who measured us on declines by country, and we didn't know he existed. Our relationship was built on the old buyer's criteria, and nobody re-sold the account to the new one.
trigger.messaging: Give account teams a 'new payments leader' play that opens with that customer's own declines by country before they pull the numbers themselves, instead of a developer-led story (M2) the new buyer doesn't care about.

evidence.excerpt: Stefan recommended it and the CFO approved.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: this went to the CFO two weeks ago.
evidence.label: quote

evidence.excerpt: I can't take an average to my CFO.
evidence.label: quote

decider.insight: The CFO was the economic approver, and as far as the transcript shows we never reached them. Stefan was effectively building a CFO case, and he told us plainly that an average uplift figure couldn't go in it. The transcript doesn't establish whether our analysis reached the CFO before approval.
decider.messaging: Package acceptance proof as a CFO-ready, customer-specific page (their markets, their approvals, the money at stake) that a payments lead can forward upward, not a product deck.

evidence.excerpt: Adyen ran a test on a slice of their international traffic and came back with results by country.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: local acquiring.
evidence.label: quote

evidence.excerpt: I can't tell you what the test showed. He wouldn't share it.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: They got very specific. What's our approval rate in this country, on this card type, by issuer. And why.
evidence.label: fact

competitor.insight: Adyen didn't win on a claim. It won on a live test with results in his own traffic, which set the terms: by country, card type and issuer, with reasons. After that, any general or average claim from us was going to lose. We still don't know what the test showed, so we can't say whether Adyen actually performed better or simply showed up with specifics first.
competitor.messaging: Answer 'local acquiring' with our own offer to test or analyze the customer's traffic by country and issuer, and with a clear per-market statement of how we handle local cards (confirm with product what we can truthfully claim).

evidence.excerpt: The Authorization Boost deck. The average uplift customers see. Adaptive Acceptance, the machine learning piece.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: that's an average. What's mine?
evidence.label: quote

evidence.excerpt: Silence was the uplift number, like I said.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: They like the product. The developers love us, billing works, nobody wanted to rip anything out. That's why the US stayed.
evidence.label: opinion

message.insight: The rep says 'we weren't really pitching,' yet we answered a buyer asking about his own approvals with M4's average uplift, and it was rejected outright. The developer and billing goodwill (M2, M7) may have protected the US, but that is the rep's read and it was irrelevant to the half of the account that left. The declined roadmap session shows he wanted his numbers now, not future features.
message.messaging: Rewrite M4 so it leads with the customer's own approval rates and a promise to diagnose them ('here is yours'), with the average uplift kept only as supporting proof.

evidence.excerpt: I don't think there was a moment. It was kind of decided before we got in the room.
evidence.label: opinion

evidence.excerpt: When the renewal notice went out and Stefan replied asking to split the contract.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: But that landed three weeks after he asked, and by then the test was finished.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: I heard from Stripe when I said I was leaving.
evidence.label: quote

decided.insight: There was a moment: the three weeks between Stefan's request and our analysis, while Adyen's test ran to completion. The rep's 'nothing to do' contradicts her own report that the analysis had fixable findings and that Stefan called it the most useful thing we'd sent. Before that, with no business review in nine or ten months and first contact only at the split request, we let the evaluation start without us.
decided.messaging: Stop positioning acceptance as a renewal-time defense and make it a standing, proactive offer: an approvals review in the customer's own numbers delivered before they ask.

evidence.excerpt: A market-by-market view of their own approval rates, with reasons.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: He asked who at Stripe looks at his numbers every month, and I didn't have a name.
evidence.label: fact

evidence.excerpt: Real findings. Things we could have fixed. He said it was the most useful thing we'd sent him.
evidence.label: fact

gaps.insight: The gap was not capability. We could produce the analysis, and it was good. The gaps were speed and ownership: three weeks to answer, and no named person who watches his numbers every month. M5's tiered response times answer a ticket question, not the 'who owns my numbers' question he actually asked.
gaps.messaging: Add a named payments-performance owner and a monthly per-market approvals review to how we position support, and say it in his words ('someone who looks at your numbers every month') instead of response-time tiers.

evidence.excerpt: Money left on the table.
evidence.label: quote

evidence.excerpt: Local cards, local rails.
evidence.label: quote

evidence.excerpt: what's mine.
evidence.label: quote

evidence.excerpt: He doesn't say 'authorization,' he says 'approvals.'
evidence.label: fact

language.insight: His frame is money and ownership ('money left on the table', 'what's mine'), while ours is product features (Authorization Boost, Adaptive Acceptance, uplift). 'Local cards, local rails' shows he thinks in terms of local acquiring infrastructure per market, a framing we had no answer to; the rep says she wouldn't know what to pitch against it.
language.messaging: Use 'approvals' and 'money left on the table' in acceptance messaging, for example 'see the approvals you're losing, market by market, in your own data', and drop the 'average uplift' headline.

gaps.question: Which international markets looked bad, and how bad?
gaps.follow_up: Ask the payments performance team to share which markets their analysis flagged, and ask Elena whether Stefan will confirm Brazil and the European markets he mentioned.

gaps.question: What did Adyen's test show?
gaps.follow_up: Ask Elena to ask Stefan whether he will share even the headline difference by country, now that the decision is made.

gaps.question: When did you first feel this was lost, and what happened right before?
gaps.follow_up: Ask Elena to walk through the timeline from the split request to the CFO approval, including exactly when she sent our analysis relative to the end of the test and the CFO decision.

gaps.question: Did our analysis reach the CFO before approval?
gaps.follow_up: Ask Elena whether Stefan included our findings in what went to the CFO.

gaps.question: Who exactly took the international volume, and was it all international traffic?
gaps.follow_up: Ask Elena to confirm with Stefan whether Adyen was selected and what share of the roughly half that was international actually moved.

gaps.question: Which part of our pitch got a positive reaction?
gaps.follow_up: Ask Elena what Stefan responded to positively, beyond the late analysis, and whether the US decision was ever discussed with him explicitly.

gaps.question: What could we have said against local acquiring?
gaps.follow_up: Ask product and payments leadership what we can truthfully claim on local acquiring by market, and build a battlecard from it.

close.rep_takeaway: When a payments owner leaves, treat the account as up for grabs: find the replacement, bring them their own approvals by market before they pull the numbers themselves, and put a named person on their numbers. Our analysis here had fixable findings and Stefan called it the most useful thing we sent, but it landed three weeks after he asked and after the competitor's test was done. Timing and ownership lost this, not the product.
